newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu to attend Gabon summit, veiled Zaire exit?.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to attend Gabon summit, veiled Zaire exit?.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko, battling cancer and rebel advances, leaves Zaire on Wednesday for a regional summit in Gabon with many people in the capital Kinshasa speculating that he is going for good.

The Mobutu spokesman who announced the departure on Tuesday insisted that the veteran leader, who has dominated Africa's third largest nation for over three decades, would be back in his capital on Friday.

But with Laurent Kabila's rebels saying they have the teeming city in their sights, newspapers in the city and ordinary Zaireans speculated that Mobutu would take advantage of the meeting to slip quietly into exile.

"Will Mobutu finally agree to go?" a headline in the opposition newspaper La Tempete asked. "The departure of Mobutu will avert the worst for Zaireans impoverished by 32 years of dictatorship," it said.

The independent La Reference Plus described Mobutu's departure as an "organised flight" linked to the rebel advance. "Sources suggest that the departure of Field Marshall Mobutu from Zaire could be definitive," it said.

Ordinary Zaireans, apprehensive about what will happen if Mobutu decides to stand and fight, clutched at the prospect he might leave for good. Many, hungry for change, openly welcome the prospect of the rebels' arrival.
At the United Nations in New York, diplomats said they hoped Mobutu would "do the right thing" -- stand down.
"The president will go to Libreville on Wednesday and will return on Friday," spokesman Kabuya Lumuna said on Tuesday without giving a precise schedule.
A Mobutu aide, who asked not to be named, said it would be wrong to interpret the president's departure as a flight into exile. Mobutu, he recalled, had repeatedly ruled out fleeing.
A government statement said Mobutu would meet the presidents of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon in Libreville.

The talks were a follow-up to a weekend peace summit between Mobutu, Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mandela on a South African ship in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire, it added. That meeting proved inconclusive.

Mobutu, 66, has seen his hold over Africa's third largest nation broken by a whirlwind rebel offensive. Kabila and his commanders, who took up arms in October, say they are building for a final push against the capital.

Zaire's government says its forces have counter-attacked and are battling to retake the town of Kikwit but independent sources say the belated army counter-thrust was near Kenge, closer to Kinshasa. Rebel radio said on Tuesday it had driven back the counter-attack in a "brief but heavy encounter".
Diplomatic sources say the front line is close to the strategic Kwango River bridge 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.
South African Vice-President Thabo Mbeki and U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson held talks in Pretoria on Tuesday on ways to avert a battle for Kinshasa.
Mbeki later announced plans to visit Zaire and five nations in the region to keep peace talks on track. Richardson left enroute to Paris for talks on the crisis.
U.N. agencies stepped up security in Kinshasa, evacuating the last non-essential staff, a senior U.N. source said.

On the humanitarian front, 1,200 Rwandan Hutu refugees who were to be airlifted home arrived safely by train in Zaire's third city of Kisangani on Tuesday -- the first such trip since 92 were killed in a stampede on Sunday.
The U.N. has flown home nearly 10,000 Hutus since launching the airlift on April 27 -- 1,976 of them on Tuesday.
